column4: Those who sell worldly life for the hereafter are summoned to fight, making the rightly directed exchange the inverse of buying this life at the next life's expense.
The warning against seeking the fleeting goods of worldly life adds that abundant gains are with God, correcting both the object and measure of the choice.
Whoever wants worldly reward is reminded that both worldly and otherworldly reward are with God, exposing the needless narrowness of choosing only the nearer portion.
People deceived by worldly life turn religion into play and diversion; the command to leave them and remind by the Quran ties the bad preference to its reckoning.
Their portion is only brief enjoyment in the world, followed by return to God and severe punishment, directly measuring the chosen object against its sequel.
After Joseph receives worldly authority, وَلَأَجْرُ ٱلْءَاخِرَةِ خَيْرٌ preserves the section's hierarchy even within a story of justified earthly success.
People rejoice in worldly life although its enjoyment compared with the hereafter is only slight, while the same ayah locates provision under God's measure.
The Prophet is told not to extend his eyes toward the enjoyments given to groups of people, a close repeated formulation of 20:131's refusal of worldly display.
The righteous believer is promised a good life and a reward according to the best deeds, showing how 16:96's lasting divine store can include rightly ordered present life.
A brief enjoyment is followed by painful punishment, compressing the passing lower portion and its enduring cost.
The Prophet is commanded to remain with those who call on their Lord and not let his eyes pass beyond them in desire for worldly adornment.
The wealthy man enters his garden wronging himself and declares that it will never perish, explicitly mistaking attractive property for permanence.
He doubts the Hour yet expects an even better return if restored to his Lord, showing the wrong chooser also misappropriating the word “better.”
His produce is encompassed and he wrings his hands over what he spent while the garden lies collapsed, turning the selected display into waste.
The question about those greatest in loss introduces a sorting whose rejected side does not recognize itself.
Their striving is lost in worldly life while they think they are doing well, exactly portraying refuse mistakenly selected as good work.
وَٱلْبَٰقِيَٰتُ ٱلصَّٰلِحَٰتُ خَيْرٌ repeats the union of remaining good and superior value, while God increases the guided in guidance.
A person who meets God's good promise is contrasted with one merely given worldly enjoyment and then brought for judgment, continuing 28:60's comparison as two human outcomes.
كُلُّ شَىْءٍ هَالِكٌ إِلَّا وَجْهَهُۥ gives the absolute boundary between everything perishing and God alone remaining.
The repeated command not to let worldly life deceive warns that present appearance can corrupt the choice made for the coming day.
God's promise is true, so worldly life must not deceive; the same formula directly pits deceptive nearness against promised reality.
Silver and gold adornment are declared no more than worldly enjoyment, while the hereafter with the Lord belongs to the God-fearing.
After worldly vegetation becomes debris in 57:20, the command to race toward forgiveness and a vast garden identifies what should be actively selected.
Noah refuses to say that those whom elite eyes despise will receive no good from God, directly overturning the classification of poor believers as refuse.
Shuayb commands full measure and weight with justice and forbids diminishing people's goods, establishing the clean dealing whose divine remainder is better in 11:86.
Noah answers the charge about lowly followers by denying knowledge of their deeds, refusing the chiefs' superficial basis for sorting them.
Their account belongs only to the Lord, relocating judgment of the supposed human refuse to the one who knows their worth.
People may dislike what is good for them and love what is bad for them; divine knowledge therefore corrects desire as a sufficient rule of selection.
Charity ruined by reproach and display becomes dust on a smooth rock swept bare by rain, a deed chosen for appearance turning into residue with no yield.
Sincere spending is a high garden whose rain multiplies its produce, the fruitful counterpart to 2:264's stripped rock.
A life of a thousand years would still not remove the covetous person from punishment, exposing mere longevity as counterfeit permanence.
A believing slave is better than an admired polytheist, correcting a chooser who confuses social station or attraction with worth.
God makes usury waste away and causes charities to grow, distinguishing wealth that looks productive from clean giving that truly increases.
Captives are told that good known in their hearts can bring them something better than what was taken, placing superior replacement beyond seized property.
The king says of Joseph, أَسْتَخْلِصْهُ لِنَفْسِى, a concrete act of selecting and reserving someone for oneself like the source dictionary's “setting apart” sense.
وَٱصْطَنَعْتُكَ لِنَفْسِى addresses Moses as one formed and set apart for God, a nonlexical enactment of reserving a chosen person to oneself.
The people build monumental structures as though they might live forever, another explicit attempt to extract permanence from worldly possession.
Solomon rejects the envoys' gift because what God has given him is better than what they offer; their delight in the gift reveals the lesser valuation.
Usury given to increase through people's wealth does not increase with God, while alms seeking God's face are the true multipliers.
People infer immunity from punishment from greater wealth and children, making abundance their false proof of chosen status.
God expands and restricts provision, but most people do not know; possession therefore cannot bear the value assigned to it in 34:35.
Neither wealth nor children bring people near to God; faith and right action instead receive multiplied reward and secure chambers.
The command to follow the best of what the Lord has sent down makes discernment of the best an urgent act before punishment arrives.
The owners of the garden are made a test when they swear to harvest it in the morning, beginning a scene in which ownership and selection are morally exposed.
They make no exception for God's will, marking the self-enclosed claim beneath their confidence in the crop.
The garden becomes like a dark, harvested field overnight, turning the expected choice produce into unusable residue.
The owners whisper that no poor person is to enter the garden, revealing that their intended harvest excludes rather than selflessly prefers the needy.
They go out convinced of their power to withhold, the wrong preference immediately before discovering the field's ruin.
On seeing the garden they first think they have lost the way, because the selected property is no longer recognizable.
They then confess that they are deprived, reversing their plan to deprive the poor.
They hope their Lord will replace the garden with one better than it, turning loss into a newly corrected request for the better portion.
The passage concludes that worldly punishment is like this but the punishment of the hereafter is greater, measuring the ruined crop against the lasting consequence.
The weighing on that day is true, and those whose scales are heavy are the successful, literally staging one pan and its selected outcome.
Those whose scales are light have lost themselves through wronging the signs, the discarded side of the same weighing.
Heavy scales identify the successful, repeating the selection-by-weight that the section evokes with its two pans.
Light scales identify those who lose themselves and remain in hell, completing the opposed result.
A person with heavy scales begins the surah's compact two-pan sorting.
A pleasing life is the result assigned to the heavy scales.
Light scales introduce the rejected side of the same valuation.
The abyss becomes the light-scaled person's home, completing the choice's terminal contrast.
Full measure and straight weighing are called better and best in outcome, joining honest valuation to the comparative good.
Whatever good people send ahead for themselves will be found with God, so present goods are retained by being transferred toward Him.
God records what people send ahead and the آثار they leave behind, giving the preference root's “traces” family a concrete relation to what remains.
Abraham makes the declaration a remaining word among his descendants, an enduring good residue meant to bring later people back.
Whatever good people send ahead for themselves will be found with God as something better and greater in reward.
Iblis claims أَنَا۠ خَيْرٌ مِّنْهُ on the basis of fire versus clay, showing “better” corrupted into material self-preference.
ٱلْعُدْوَةِ ٱلدُّنْيَا means the nearer bank opposite the farther bank, a spatial use that bounds the section's low-value reading of the d-n-w family.
The unbelievers' word is made the lowest while God's word is the highest, reversing earthly power through an explicit high/low judgment.
وَمَا كَانَ رَبُّكَ نَسِيًّا excludes forgetfulness from the Lord, bounding the discarded-object sense attached to created beings.
Moses says his Lord neither errs nor forgets, distinguishing divine preservation of the record from human forgetting and abandonment.
أَدْنَى ٱلْأَرْضِ locates the Romans' defeat in the nearer land, preserving the root's spatial sense rather than a judgment of baseness.
ٱلسَّمَآءَ ٱلدُّنْيَا is the nearest heaven adorned with stars, a repeated nonmoral use of the same adjective as worldly life.
Iblis again calls himself better than Adam from their materials, a repeated warning that comparative “good” can voice arrogant misvaluation.
The nearest heaven is adorned with lamps, confirming that dunyā can mark proximity without calling its noun morally low.
The nearest heaven is adorned with lamps, another exact boundary on deriving moral worth from the adjective alone.
The Prophet is told not to be deceived by unbelievers' free movement through the lands, introducing the apparent worldly advantage corrected in 3:197-198.
That movement is only a little enjoyment followed by hell, supplying the passing side before 3:198 names what is better with God.
God chose Abraham in the world and places him among the righteous in the hereafter, joining divine selection across the two lives.
God's selection of Adam, Noah, and Abraham's and Imran's houses over the worlds supplies a direct scene of the chooser and the chosen.
God tells Moses that He selected him over the people by His messages and speech, making right preference an informed divine act.
God selects messengers from angels and humans, another explicit selection whose criterion belongs to the all-hearing, all-seeing chooser.
Giving cherished wealth to relatives, orphans, needy people, travelers, petitioners, and captives concretely enacts preferring needy others over possession.
Wisdom is called خَيْرًا كَثِيرًا, pairing goodness with abundance while locating that abundance in discernment rather than property.
The expenditure of rejecters is compared to a freezing wind that destroys a crop, another field image in which apparent stored value becomes loss.
Rejecters' deeds are like a desert mirage that the thirsty person takes for water but finds to be nothing, a specific false selection by appearance.
Many settlements exulting in their livelihood are destroyed, leaving dwellings scarcely inhabited and inherited by God; plentiful provision becomes abandoned remainder.
Qarun's immense treasure and oppressive conduct establish the abundance whose value 28:77-82 subsequently overturns.
Qarun attributes his wealth to his own knowledge, claiming a corrupt source of merit for the property others will desire in 28:79.
After the flood, Noah's descendants are made the surviving remainder, a human remnant preserved from a destroyed world.
